text: KVOS-TV (channel 12) is a television station licensed to Bellingham, Washington, United States, serving the Seattle–Tacoma market as an affiliate of the Spanish-language network Univision. It is owned by Weigel Broadcasting alongside Seattle-licensed MeTV owned-and-operated station KFFV, channel 44 (which KVOS simulcasts on its third digital subchannel). Its other subchannels carry Weigel's other diginet concepts. Though it now functions as a Seattle-market station, for much of its history it primarily served an audience in southwestern British Columbia, Canada, including Vancouver and Victoria. KVOS-TV's transmitter is located atop Mount Constitution on Orcas Island in the San Juan Islands, at an altitude of 2,621 feet (799 m) above the adjacent terrain. The station's signal is very well received throughout the British Columbia Lower Mainland, southern Vancouver Island, and much of northwest Washington. KVOS-TV's original studios were on Ellis Street in Bellingham; however, after its sale to OTA Broadcasting in 2010, the Bellingham facility was closed and the station currently shares studios with KFFV on Third Avenue South in Seattle. KVOS at one time maintained offices in Burnaby, British Columbia, and before that on West 7th Avenue in Vancouver, but no longer has a physical presence in the Vancouver area. KVOS signed on June 3, 1953, owned by Bellingham businessman Rogan Jones along with KVOS radio (AM 790, now KGMI), who had owned the radio station since 1928 and was known for a case establishing broadcasters' right to the same news reports as newspapers. Its first broadcast was a kinescope of Queen Elizabeth II's coronation, the day before. Since Canada had no television stations west of Ontario at that time (Vancouver would get its own locally-operated station in CBC outlet CBUT that December), the British government flew film of the BBC's coverage to Vancouver, where the Mounties escorted it to the border, and the Washington State Patrol drove it to Bellingham. The station's original slogan was "Your Peace Arch Station, serving Northwest Washington and British Columbia." KVOS initially faced financial difficulties despite Jones believing he could support a television station in a city the size of Bellingham. He built a powerful transmitter on Orcas Island to reach Seattle, but even with increased power, it did not cover enough of the Seattle area to solve the problem. Revenues from the radio station were the only thing keeping channel 12 afloat. In 1955, Jones, recognizing most of his audience was across the border, incorporated KVOS in Canada, establishing a subsidiary, KVOS-TV Limited, which brought in revenue by allowing Vancouver-area businesses to buy advertising time. KVOS-TV continued to broadcast from Bellingham, with much of its audience based in southwestern British Columbia. After nine years of ownership, Jones sold the station to Miami-based Wometco Enterprises in 1962. Prior to Canadian content regulations in the early 1970s, Canadian television stations typically spent little on domestic production, making KVOS's Vancouver production office one of the largest Canadian production studios anywhere, particularly through its Canawest Film Studios division, and employing more Canadian writers, actors, artists, and musicians than any other media organization in Canada besides the CBC, according to Vancouver MP Simma Holt. The station was further harmed by a 1976 change in Canadian tax law, which prevented Canadian companies from writing off advertising purchased on American stations as a tax deduction. In an effort to stop the change, KVOS proposed an exemption on the condition it return $2 million per year to Canadian television production; the proposal failed, but the station survived by closing its Canadian production office and reducing advertising rates to offset the tax increase advertisers would face. Even into the 1990s, the station was sometimes criticized in CRTC licensing hearings for allegedly draining advertising revenue from Vancouver stations; CKVU-TV president Daryl Duke once compared KVOS to smallpox. Dave Mintz, a minority investor since 1955 and president since 1961, left in 1979 to become president of Canada's fledgling Global Television Network. Although American by birth, due to the importance of Vancouver operations, Mintz resided full-time in Vancouver when he took the Global job. KVOS began as a DuMont affiliate upon sign-on in 1953 and remained so until DuMont went off the air in 1956. From January 1, 1955, until about 1979, it was a primary CBS affiliate. In the late 1970s, KVOS sharply reduced CBS programming due to two commercial disputes: first, Seattle's CBS affiliate KIRO-TV filed complaints about duplicate transmission of CBS programming in the Seattle market; second, CRTC regulations aimed at increasing Canadian content and reducing American network affiliates on cable systems in Canada put pressure on the station. While KVOS nominally retained its CBS affiliation until 1987, carrying a few CBS programs like 60 Minutes, it transitioned into an independent station that primarily aired a diverse mix of syndicated and locally produced programming, including locally produced news and public affairs. Beginning in 1990, it carried programs syndicated from Toronto-based independent station Citytv, whose owner CHUM Limited did not yet have a station in Vancouver. Wometco was bought by Kohlberg Kravis Roberts in 1984 and sold off in 1985, with KVOS sold to Ackerley Communications. In the early 1990s, due to FCC syndicated exclusivity rules affecting the Seattle market, KVOS was dropped from most Seattle cable systems. For part of this era, the station used both Canadian and American TV ratings at the start of each program and was believed to be the only station on either side of the border to do so. Since at least early 2007, only U.S. ratings have been shown. In 2001, CHUM Limited purchased CKVU-TV from Canwest, turning it into a local version of Citytv in 2002 and beginning to air CHUM-provided programming on September 1, 2001, and launched a new station in Victoria known as CIVI-TV. The launch of these outlets, along with major affiliation and ownership changes in the Vancouver–Victoria market in September 2001, caused KVOS to be displaced by CIVI from its long-time home on channel 12 on many Vancouver-area cable systems and led to the loss of Citytv as a programming source. The station came under Clear Channel Communications (now iHeartMedia) in 2003 following the purchase of Ackerley. On November 16, 2006, Clear Channel announced it would sell its entire television division, including KVOS-TV, after being acquired by private equity firms. On April 20, 2007, Clear Channel entered into an agreement to sell its entire television stations group to Providence Equity Partners' Newport Television. Providence initially announced it would not keep KVOS or KFTY in Santa Rosa, California, instead reselling them to LK Station Group, but LK could not obtain financing, so KVOS remained with Newport (KFTY was eventually sold to High Plains Broadcasting, now owned by Innovate Corp. as KEMO-TV). In 2008, KVOS filed an application to the FCC to build its digital facility in Granite Falls, Snohomish County (48°08′09″N 121°58′56″W / 48.13583°N 121.98222°W / 48.13583; -121.98222). The proposed location would have provided city-grade coverage of most of the Seattle area while remaining within 15 miles (24 km) of Bellingham, as required by FCC rules, but would have significantly diminished its reach into Canada. The application was dismissed on July 16, 2009. In January 2010, KVOS swapped channel positions (now on channel 30) with TSN on Shaw Cable in Metro Vancouver. In Vancouver, KVOS is not included on Shaw's "basic" lineup but is included as channel 30 on Shaw's "classic" and "digital" lineups. In Victoria, KVOS is included only on Shaw's "digital" lineup, on channel 69. In October 2010, KVOS was added to Comcast's digital lineup on channel 72 in the Seattle–Tacoma area—marking the first time in 20 years the station has been seen in Seattle proper and the first time it has been viewed in parts of Southwest Washington and Gray's Harbor coastal communities of Aberdeen and Hoquiam. The station became an affiliate of the classic television network MeTV on April 25, 2011. Later, TheCoolTV was added as a subchannel of KVOS on August 18, 2011. Unlike the main 12.1 feed, the 12.2 feed was not carried on any Canadian cable system. In January 2014, TheCoolTV was dropped in favor of Movies!. Newport agreed to sell KVOS to OTA Broadcasting, LLC, controlled by Michael Dell's MSD Capital, in December 2011. The deal created a duopoly in the Seattle market with KFFV. OTA Broadcasting assumed control of KVOS on March 6, 2012. As a result, most of KVOS' staff was laid off, and most of the operations staff were moved to Seattle. In September 2013, subchannel 12.3 was added, airing the Canadian Punjabi language specialty channel Sur Sagar TV, which was dropped in mid-2015 and the feed went dark until September 5, 2016, when it began broadcasting Heroes & Icons (H&I). On March 12, 2015, the main feed of KVOS adopted KFFV's 44.6 feed, the branding was switched from MeTV KVOS to MeTV Seattle, the ident was MeTV KVOS-KFFV, and advertising was shared between KVOS and KFFV. Due to WeatherNation TV previously airing on KFFV, Comcast identified the station as KFFVVW on its on-screen guide. Weigel Broadcasting agreed to acquire KVOS-TV and KFFV, along with KAXT-CD and KTLN-TV in San Francisco, in a $23.2 million deal on October 18, 2017, giving Weigel control of both of its MeTV affiliates in the Puget Sound region. The sale was closed on January 15, 2018, with KVOS and sister station KFFV now under Weigel ownership. On January 17, 2018, H&I became KVOS's primary network and moved to subchannel 12.1, MeTV was relocated to subchannel 12.3, and new offering Decades was added to subchannel 12.4. KVOS' lineup expanded on September 3, 2018, when Start TV was added to subchannel 12.5. MeTV Plus was added to subchannel 12.6 on September 27, 2021. On March 28, 2022, Story Television launched on subchannel 12.7. In April 2019, the CRTC approved a request by Shaw Cable in Kelowna, British Columbia, to add KVOS-DT3 to its systems on a discretionary basis. Shaw felt the switch to Heroes & Icons was at odds with its authorization to carry the MeTV programming feed. There was no objection from the only local station in the market (which, however, is owned by a corporate sibling). During the 2023 holiday season, Weigel quietly updated the station's website to reflect Univision would move to KVOS's main channel from Sinclair Broadcast Group's KUNS-TV (channel 51), which became an affiliate of The CW on January 1, 2024. As a result, H&I moved from subchannel 12.1 to subchannel 12.8. With KVOS's unique status, Univision's domestic schedule became available over-the-air in Vancouver, Victoria, and southwest British Columbia for the first time; Univision has a partnership with TLN to operate a licensed specialty channel, Univision Canada, featuring its programming. Until January 14, 2018, KVOS ran a variety of religious and paid programs, as well as other features between shows including On Scene and MeEvents. KVOS has produced a variety of local shows over the years. The religious program Anchor first aired in 1968 with host Pastor Leonard Ericksen and ran for 30 years, becoming one of the longest-running shows of its kind on television. KVOS also produced many news, feature, public affairs, and informational programs. The 10:30 Report, Weeks End, and Cana West helped launch the careers of well-known names such as Andy Anderson and Al Swift, who both went on to successful political careers. Other feature programs included Kids Stuff, Pacific Style, Pacific Issues, Sports Probe, To Serve and Protect, and Red's Classic Theatre with famed B.C. radio personality Red Robinson from 1989 to 2001. Another famous B.C. radio personality, Jack Cullen, hosted Owl Prowl Television Theatre in the 1950s; two reels of footage from that show are held by the City of Vancouver Archives. During the 1970s and 1980s, KVOS aired a number of British comedy programs each evening, such as On the Buses, The Benny Hill Show, Dave Allen at Large, and The Two Ronnies. It was also the only non-PBS (and only commercial) station in the U.S. to air Doctor Who from 1983 to 1993. On the morning of May 21, 1990, NewsView began broadcasts, originally starting as a half-hour show. NewsView featured a variety of local and regional news, sports, and weather for northwest Washington and the border communities of British Columbia. The first anchor was Cyndy Glenn, followed by Michele Higgins, Susan Cowden, Crystal King, Cara Buckingham, and Ty Ray. Reporters included Jeff Wyngaert, Amy Cloud, Dave Sienko, and Joe Bates, while weather duties were covered (in the early years) by Jeff Kelly and Dave George, then Dan Leniczek, Dave Sienko, and Greg Otterholt. The newscast debuted at 6:30 a.m. and eventually expanded to a 90-minute show from 6:30 to 8 a.m. Due to low advertising revenues, KVOS ended NewsView on January 23, 2007, after 16½ years. Various syndicated programs replaced it in the 6:30–8 a.m. time slots. Alongside NewsView, KVOS broadcast hourly weather updates and local forecasts at the top of every hour, under the title WeatherView; these updates were introduced in the 1980s and ended by the mid-2000s. KVOS began airing Northwest Notebook, hosted by Ty Ray, in February 2007. The show featured interviews with newsmakers from Northwest Washington and the Lower Mainland. Ray also hosted Daily Planner, a community calendar that aired six times a day. It has since gone off the air. The station's signal is multiplexed: KVOS-TV shut down its analog signal over VHF channel 12 on February 17, 2009, as part of the federally mandated transition from analog to digital television (which Congress had moved to June 12 the previous month). The station's digital signal remained on its pre-transition UHF channel 35, using virtual channel 12. As a result of the FCC's 600 MHz auction, KVOS moved to channel 14 due to spectrum repacking on October 19, 2019.

The station's digital signal continued to broadcast on its original UHF channel 35, designated with a virtual channel 12. As a result of the FCC's 600 MHz auction, KVOS relocated to channel 14 because of spectrum repacking, which took place on October 19, 2019.
